questions.stem: Which process carries heating energy through solids?

options.explanation: Conduction is the main heating transfer route in solids.
Radiation passes through, but conduction dominates in solids.
Evaporation is a change of state, not the solid heating route.
Convection needs a fluid; it cannot happen in solids.

questions.stem: Which group of materials conducts heat best?

options.explanation: Gases are extremely poor conductors.
Metals are extremely good thermal conductors.
Liquids are poor conductors.
Non-metals are poor conductors.

questions.stem: What makes a material a good insulator?

options.explanation: Metals are the best conductors, not insulators.
That describes a conductor.

options.text: does not transfer energy by heating
options.explanation: Insulators stop the conduction route.
Free electrons belong to metals and speed conduction.

questions.stem: Why is trapped air such a good insulator?

options.text: air reflects heat like a mirror
options.explanation: Reflection is the shiny-surface behaviour for radiation.

options.text: air has no particles at all
options.explanation: Air is full of particles; they are just far apart.
Nothing absorbs and destroys energy.

options.text: air is a gas, so it conducts very slowly, and when trapped it cannot move to form convection currents
options.explanation: Both halves make trapped air special.

questions.stem: Why does conduction pull energy from bare feet faster through tiles than through a rug?

options.text: the tiles conduct energy from the feet faster than the rug does
options.explanation: Better conduction pulls heat from the feet faster, so tiles feel colder.

options.text: the rug heats the feet by radiation
options.explanation: The rug insulates; it does not actively heat.
The rug has no energy source.

options.text: the tiles are colder than the rug
options.explanation: Both sit at room temperature.

questions.stem: State what poor conductors are called.
questions.modelAnswer: Poor conductors are called insulators — materials that do not transfer energy by heating.

questions.stem: State what happens to the atoms of a substance when it is heated.
questions.modelAnswer: Heated atoms vibrate harder, knock into their neighbours and hand energy along from atom to atom.

questions.stem: Explain why a woolly hat keeps a head warm even though wool itself is not a heat source.
questions.modelAnswer: Wool traps air in small pockets. The air is a gas, so it conducts heat away from the head very slowly, and because the air is trapped it cannot circulate to carry energy off by convection either — so the head loses energy to the surroundings much more slowly.

questions.stem: A saucepan has a metal body and a plastic handle. Explain the choice of material for each part.
questions.modelAnswer: The body is metal because conduction must transfer energy from the hob to the food quickly; the handle is plastic because conduction into the hand must be slow, and plastics are poor conductors — good insulators.

questions.stem: When one end of a metal rod is heated, how does energy reach the far end?

options.text: the hot atoms travel along the rod
options.explanation: Atoms stay in place; only energy travels.

options.text: atoms vibrate more and pass energy on through collisions, helped by delocalised electrons
options.explanation: Both mechanisms carry the energy.

options.text: the rod melts gradually from the hot end
options.explanation: Melting is a change of state, not conduction.

options.text: infra-red light carries the energy inside the rod
options.explanation: Radiation is not the internal route here.

questions.stem: What special particles do metals contain that non-metals lack, speeding conduction?

options.explanation: Protons are bound in nuclei in every solid.
Neutrons stay in nuclei everywhere.
Metals’ free electrons collide with atoms and speed the transfer.
The lattice is atoms, not free neutrons.

questions.stem: Why does the lattice alone conduct more slowly than a metal’s full mechanism?

options.explanation: Non-metals have atoms; they lack free electrons.
Temperature is the condition, not the mechanism.
Vibration is exactly what they do.

options.text: collision-to-collision transfer through the lattice is slower than the extra electron collisions
options.explanation: Electrons add a faster parallel route.

questions.stem: A metal spoon in hot soup becomes too hot to hold while a wooden spoon does not. The key difference is:

options.text: metal’s delocalised electrons conduct the soup’s energy up the handle quickly
options.explanation: Fast conduction is the metal’s behaviour.
Absorption of liquid is not the thermal point here.

options.text: metal has a lower melting point
options.explanation: Nothing melts in this scenario.
Wood is solid; the difference is the material, not a hole.

questions.stem: Which row correctly orders conduction speed through the same shape of bar?

options.explanation: The material decides the rate.

options.text: copper bar > plastic bar > air gap
options.explanation: Metal, then non-metal solid, then gas — fastest to slowest.

options.text: air gap > copper bar > plastic bar
options.explanation: Air is the worst conductor of the three.

options.text: plastic bar > copper bar > air gap
options.explanation: Metal beats plastic.

questions.stem: State what the delocalised electrons in a metal do to help thermal conduction.
questions.modelAnswer: They crash into the metal’s atoms, handing the vibrations along through the material, which moves heat faster.

questions.stem: State what happens to the spacing of particles in a material that is very dense, and its effect on conduction.
questions.modelAnswer: Denser materials pack their particles nearer together, so the collision chain passes energy along more easily.

questions.stem: Explain why a metal chain feels colder than a rope left overnight in the same cold shed.
questions.modelAnswer: Both sit at the shed’s temperature, but the metal’s delocalised electrons conduct energy from your warm hand into the chain far faster than the rope’s non-metal lattice does, so the chain drains heat from the hand quickly and feels colder.

questions.stem: A soldering iron tip is copper but its handle is wood-effect plastic. Use conduction to explain both choices.
questions.modelAnswer: The copper tip must deliver heat to the joint quickly, and copper’s delocalised electrons make it an excellent conductor; the plastic handle must not conduct that heat to the grip, and being a poor conductor it insulates the user’s hand.

questions.stem: In which states of matter can convection occur?

options.explanation: Metals are solids; they conduct instead.
Solids cannot flow, so no convection.
Convection needs a fluid; solids are excluded.
Liquids convect too — boiling water is the classic case.

questions.stem: Why does heated fluid rise?

options.explanation: The current forms even with gentle heating.
Particles move APART when heated.

options.text: it weighs less because heating destroys particles
options.explanation: Particles are conserved; heating only spreads them.

options.text: heating makes the fluid expand, so it becomes less dense than the surrounding fluid
options.explanation: Lower density floats above higher density.

questions.stem: What completes a convection current after the hot fluid rises?

options.text: the hot fluid cools, contracts, becomes denser and sinks back down
options.explanation: The sinking return leg closes the loop.

options.text: the fluid evaporates at the top
options.explanation: Evaporation is not part of the current cycle.

options.text: the fluid turns solid at the top
options.explanation: Nothing freezes in a convection current demonstration.

options.text: the fluid stays at the top forever
options.explanation: It cools at the top and returns.

questions.stem: A radiator warms a room mainly through which transfer process — conduction, convection or radiation?

options.text: conduction through the air, because air conducts well
options.explanation: Air conducts very poorly.

options.text: convection: warm air rises from the radiator, cools and circulates
options.explanation: The room-wide circulation is a convection current.
Radiation contributes, but the room-wide warming is convective.
Condensation is a change of state, not the warming route.

questions.stem: Why does a sea breeze blow from the sea towards the land on a hot day? Answer using convection.

options.text: the wind is caused by waves pushing air
options.explanation: Waves are a result of wind, not its cause.

options.text: cold air rises from the sea
options.explanation: Cold air sinks.

options.text: the land heats the air above it, which rises, and cooler air from the sea moves in to replace it
options.explanation: The land-side updraught pulls the sea breeze ashore.

options.text: the sea heats the air above it, which rises towards the land
options.explanation: Water heats slowly; the land is the hot side.

questions.stem: State what happens to the density of a fluid when it is heated, and the immediate effect.
questions.modelAnswer: Heated fluid expands, becoming less dense than the surroundings, so it rises.

questions.stem: State why convection cannot happen in a solid.
questions.modelAnswer: Convection needs the fluid itself to flow; solids cannot flow, so convection cannot occur in them.

questions.stem: Explain why a room warms better if the heater is placed near the floor rather than near the ceiling.
questions.modelAnswer: Warm air rises, so a floor-level heater starts its convection current through the whole room’s height: warm air climbs, cools against the ceiling and walls, and sinks back to be reheated. A ceiling-level heater warms only the top layer, which is already above the cooler air and so barely circulates.

questions.stem: A pan of water is heated gently at one side and a crystal of potassium permanganate sits above the flame. Describe what the purple trail shows.
questions.modelAnswer: The purple trail rises with the warmed water above the flame, spreads across the surface, cools, sinks at the far side and returns along the bottom to the flame — tracing the closed loop of the convection current.

questions.stem: What does every object do, whatever its temperature?

options.explanation: Convection needs a fluid; not every object is fluid.
Conduction needs contact; radiation needs nothing.
Every object also EMITS.
All bodies emit infrared all the time.

questions.stem: How does temperature affect the radiation an object emits?

options.text: the hotter the object, the more infrared it radiates in a given time
options.explanation: Emission rate rises with temperature.

options.text: temperature has no effect on emission
options.explanation: Temperature is the driver of emission rate.

options.text: only very hot objects emit any radiation
options.explanation: All bodies emit, however cool.
It is the other way round.

questions.stem: Which surface is the best absorber AND emitter of thermal radiation?

options.explanation: White is a poor absorber and emitter.
Black surfaces are the best at emitting and absorbing.
The surface quality decides.
Shiny is the worst at both — it reflects.

questions.stem: A thermos flask keeps drinks hot partly by coating surfaces with shiny metal. Why does that work?

options.text: shiny surfaces stop convection inside the liquid
options.explanation: The coating addresses radiation, not the fluid’s convection.

options.text: shiny metal conducts the heat away faster
options.explanation: The flask wants to STOP transfer, not speed it.

options.text: shiny surfaces are very poor emitters and reflect radiation back, reducing radiated loss
options.explanation: Poor emission plus reflection keeps the radiation in.
Nothing adds energy.

questions.stem: For a mug of hot coffee standing on a table, which loss route does NOT need any material between the coffee and its surroundings?

options.explanation: Evaporation needs the liquid itself to leave.
The mug wall is the material.

options.text: convection of air above the mug
options.explanation: The air is the material.

options.text: radiation from the coffee’s surface and the mug’s outside
options.explanation: Radiation crosses even a vacuum.

questions.stem: State how emission and absorption depend on the colour of a surface.
questions.modelAnswer: Black surfaces are the best emitters and absorbers; shiny surfaces are the worst at both, reflecting radiation instead.

questions.stem: State the three routes by which a hot mug of coffee loses energy to the surroundings.
questions.modelAnswer: Radiation from its surfaces, conduction through the mug walls, and convection of the warm air above it.

questions.stem: Explain why painting a car’s radiator fins matte black helps it cool the engine.
questions.modelAnswer: Matte black surfaces are the best emitters of thermal radiation, so the fins radiate the engine’s energy away at the fastest rate the surface allows; being good absorbers too does no harm, because the fins are hotter than their surroundings and the net flow is outward.

questions.stem: Two identical mugs of coffee stand on a table, one matte black and one shiny steel. State which cools faster and name the route that differs most between them.
questions.modelAnswer: The matte black mug cools faster: it is the better emitter, so the radiation route — the one that needs no medium — carries energy away from it more quickly than from the shiny mug, which reflects and poorly emits.
